power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 26 columns across 5 data files.
#### Issues Identified

5 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 5 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. info.title: llmClassificR: Text Classification with Large Language Models, Network Psychometrics, and Calibrated Uncertainty in R

author.affiliation:
Department of Psychology
								University of Virginia

text.text: The R package llmClassificR is available at https://github.com/hfgolino/llmClassificR.
text.formatted: The R package llmClassificR is available at <ref type="url" target="https://github.com/hfgolino/llmClassificR">https://github.com/hfgolino/llmClassificR</ref>.

text.text: The replication script, the GoEmotions subset, and the cached results of all analyses are available in the supplementary materials.

Classifying texts into psychologically meaningful categories is one of the oldest problems in the quantitative study of language, and one of the most consequential, since the categories assigned to open-ended survey responses, diaries, clinical notes, social media posts, or interview transcripts frequently become the variables that enter every subsequent statistical model, so that errors in the classification step propagate, often silently, to the substantive conclusions of a study (Feuerriegel et al., 2025; O. N. E. Kjell, Kjell, Garcia, & Sikström, 2019).
text.formatted: Classifying texts into psychologically meaningful categories is one of the oldest problems in the quantitative study of language, and one of the most consequential, since the categories assigned to open-ended survey responses, diaries, clinical notes, social media posts, or interview transcripts frequently become the variables that enter every subsequent statistical model, so that errors in the classification step propagate, often silently, to the substantive conclusions of a study <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Feuerriegel et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">O. N. E. Kjell, Kjell, Garcia, & Sikström, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: For several decades, the dominant approaches relied either on dictionaries, in which a text receives a score for each category based on the words it contains (Boyd, Ashokkumar, Seraj, & Pennebaker, 2022; Mohammad & Turney, 2013), or on supervised models fitted to word counts, in which a classifier learns, from texts coded by trained human raters, which words are associated with each category (Feinerer, Hornik, & Meyer, 2008; Salton & Buckley, 1988).
text.formatted: For several decades, the dominant approaches relied either on dictionaries, in which a text receives a score for each category based on the words it contains <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Boyd, Ashokkumar, Seraj, & Pennebaker, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Mohammad & Turney, 2013)</ref>, or on supervised models fitted to word counts, in which a classifier learns, from texts coded by trained human raters, which words are associated with each category <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Feinerer, Hornik, & Meyer, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b94">Salton & Buckley, 1988)</ref>.

text.text: The last decade changed this landscape in successive waves: contextual encoder models such as BERT produced representations in which the meaning of a word depends on the words around it (Devlin, Chang, Lee, & Toutanova, 2019; Vaswani et al., 2017), sentence encoders turned these representations into vectors in which texts with similar meanings lie close to each other (Reimers & Gurevych, 2019), and generative large language models (LLMs) made it possible to classify texts from nothing more than an instruction and a list of categories (Brown et al., 2020), a possibility that was rapidly adopted in psychology and the social sciences (Abdurahman et al., 2024; Demszky et al., 2023; Gilardi, Alizadeh, & Kubli, 2023; Rathje et al., 2024; Ziems et al., 2024).
text.formatted: The last decade changed this landscape in successive waves: contextual encoder models such as BERT produced representations in which the meaning of a word depends on the words around it <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Devlin, Chang, Lee, & Toutanova, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b106">Vaswani et al., 2017)</ref>, sentence encoders turned these representations into vectors in which texts with similar meanings lie close to each other <ref type="bibr" target="#b88">(Reimers & Gurevych, 2019)</ref>, and generative large language models (LLMs) made it possible to classify texts from nothing more than an instruction and a list of categories <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Brown et al., 2020)</ref>, a possibility that was rapidly adopted in psychology and the social sciences <ref type="bibr">(Abdurahman et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Demszky et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Gilardi, Alizadeh, & Kubli, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b87">Rathje et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b123">Ziems et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: A further step was taken in September 2026, when the company TypeSafe released Jev, a general-purpose classification model that does not generate text but returns probabilities for typed questions about a text (choosing one of several options, answering yes or no, or rating the text on an ordinal rubric), described by Raschka (2026) as "the ChatGPT moment for classification", since it can classify many kinds of text inputs cheaply without the need to fine-tune a custom classifier for each task (TypeSafe, 2026).
text.formatted: A further step was taken in September 2026, when the company TypeSafe released Jev, a general-purpose classification model that does not generate text but returns probabilities for typed questions about a text (choosing one of several options, answering yes or no, or rating the text on an ordinal rubric), described by <ref type="bibr" target="#b84">Raschka (2026)</ref> as "the ChatGPT moment for classification", since it can classify many kinds of text inputs cheaply without the need to fine-tune a custom classifier for each task <ref type="bibr" target="#b104">(TypeSafe, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The multiplication of strategies created new possibilities, but also new problems for researchers who want to use text classification as a measurement procedure.

The first problem is that most applications assume that the categories are known in advance, while many research questions in psychology start one step earlier, asking whether the texts organize themselves into categories at all, how many categories are supported by the data, and whether these categories correspond to the constructs proposed by a theory.

Network psychometrics offers a principled answer to this kind of question for questionnaire data, by estimating a network of partial associations between variables and detecting its communities with exploratory graph analysis (EGA; Golino & Epskamp, 2017; Borsboom et al., 2021; Golino et al., 2020), and the same logic can be applied to texts once each text is represented by an embedding vector, treating texts as nodes and their co-variation across embedding dimensions as edges.
text.formatted: Network psychometrics offers a principled answer to this kind of question for questionnaire data, by estimating a network of partial associations between variables and detecting its communities with exploratory graph analysis (EGA; <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Golino & Epskamp, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Borsboom et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Golino et al., 2020)</ref>, and the same logic can be applied to texts once each text is represented by an embedding vector, treating texts as nodes and their co-variation across embedding dimensions as edges.

text.text: Transformers, however, do not produce a single representation of a text, but one representation per layer, and the information that distinguishes psychological categories is distributed unevenly across layers (Jawahar, Sagot, & Seddah, 2019; Rogers, Kovaleva, & Rumshisky, 2020; Tenney, Das, & Pavlick, 2019), which turns the representation of a text into a multiplex network, that is, a set of networks defined on the same nodes.
text.formatted: Transformers, however, do not produce a single representation of a text, but one representation per layer, and the information that distinguishes psychological categories is distributed unevenly across layers <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Jawahar, Sagot, & Seddah, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b90">Rogers, Kovaleva, & Rumshisky, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b101">Tenney, Das, & Pavlick, 2019)</ref>, which turns the representation of a text into a multiplex network, that is, a set of networks defined on the same nodes.

text.text: Complexity science provides tools for this situation, and one of them, the prime-weight encoding of multiplex networks proposed by Santoro and Nicosia (2020) and adapted to psychological networks by Golino, Nesselroade, and Christensen (2025), is used in the present paper to combine the networks estimated from every layer of an encoder (and from embedding services) into a single network whose communities can be compared with known categories.
text.formatted: Complexity science provides tools for this situation, and one of them, the prime-weight encoding of multiplex networks proposed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b95">Santoro and Nicosia (2020)</ref> and adapted to psychological networks by <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Golino, Nesselroade, and Christensen (2025)</ref>, is used in the present paper to combine the networks estimated from every layer of an encoder (and from embedding services) into a single network whose communities can be compared with known categories.

text.text: The second problem concerns the quality of the probabilities attached to a classification.

A classifier that is right 80% of the time but reports 99% confidence for every decision, or one that cannot say which of its decisions deserve a second look, is of limited use when the classifications are treated as data (Geng et al., 2024; Guo, Pleiss, Sun, & Weinberger, 2017).
text.formatted: A classifier that is right 80% of the time but reports 99% confidence for every decision, or one that cannot say which of its decisions deserve a second look, is of limited use when the classifications are treated as data <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Geng et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Guo, Pleiss, Sun, & Weinberger, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Probabilities returned by neural networks are frequently miscalibrated (Desai & Durrett, 2020; Guo et al., 2017; Minderer et al., 2021), the confidences verbalized by generative LLMs are only partially informative (Lin, Hilton, & Evans, 2022; Tian et al., 2023; Xiong et al., 2024), and the methods that repair or certify uncertainty, such as temperature scaling (Guo et al., 2017), Platt scaling (Platt, 2000), and conformal prediction (Angelopoulos & Bates, 2023; Vovk, Gammerman, & Shafer, 2005), are rarely part of the text classification software used by applied researchers.
text.formatted: Probabilities returned by neural networks are frequently miscalibrated <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Desai & Durrett, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Guo et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">Minderer et al., 2021)</ref>, the confidences verbalized by generative LLMs are only partially informative <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(Lin, Hilton, & Evans, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b102">Tian et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b118">Xiong et al., 2024)</ref>, and the methods that repair or certify uncertainty, such as temperature scaling <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Guo et al., 2017)</ref>, Platt scaling <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">(Platt, 2000)</ref>, and conformal prediction <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Angelopoulos & Bates, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b108">Vovk, Gammerman, & Shafer, 2005)</ref>, are rarely part of the text classification software used by applied researchers.

text.text: The third problem is practical and could be called LLM engineering: generative models answer in free text, must be prompted in batches to keep costs and rate limits under control, are sensitive to the order of the texts and to the wording of the prompt (Lu, Bartolo, Moore, Riedel, & Stenetorp, 2022; Pezeshkpour & Hruschka, 2024; Sclar, Choi, Tsvetkov, & Suhr, 2024; Zhao, Wallace, Feng, Klein, & Singh, 2021), occasionally return labels that do not exist, change or are retired by their providers, and send data to external servers, all of which affect reproducibility and the ethics of a study (Abdurahman et al., 2024; Sainz et al., 2023; Ziems et al., 2024).
text.formatted: The third problem is practical and could be called LLM engineering: generative models answer in free text, must be prompted in batches to keep costs and rate limits under control, are sensitive to the order of the texts and to the wording of the prompt <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">(Lu, Bartolo, Moore, Riedel, & Stenetorp, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">Pezeshkpour & Hruschka, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b96">Sclar, Choi, Tsvetkov, & Suhr, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b121">Zhao, Wallace, Feng, Klein, & Singh, 2021)</ref>, occasionally return labels that do not exist, change or are retired by their providers, and send data to external servers, all of which affect reproducibility and the ethics of a study <ref type="bibr">(Abdurahman et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b93">Sainz et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b123">Ziems et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The package llmClassificR (Golino, 2026) for R (R Core Team, 2026) was developed to address these three problems within a single, consistent interface written for applied researchers, and was used in the 2026 edition of a course on text classification with LLMs in R. The package currently exports 75 functions and ships seven data sets.
text.formatted: The package llmClassificR <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Golino, 2026)</ref> for R (R Core Team, 2026) was developed to address these three problems within a single, consistent interface written for applied researchers, and was used in the 2026 edition of a course on text classification with LLMs in R. The package currently exports 75 functions and ships seven data sets.

text.text: It covers bag-of-words baselines; embeddings from local encoders, decoder LLMs, sentence encoders, and two embedding services (Voyage AI and Jina AI); unsupervised classification with EGA and prime-weight encoding; supervised classification heads; prompted classification with generative LLMs served by Groq, including strict JSON Schema outputs, ensembles, self-consistency, and LLM-as-judge; retrieval-augmented generation (RAG; Lewis et al., 2020) and topic discovery; Jev-based classification; do-it-yourself Jev-like classifiers; and a set of tools for calibration and uncertainty quantification.
text.formatted: It covers bag-of-words baselines; embeddings from local encoders, decoder LLMs, sentence encoders, and two embedding services <ref type="bibr">(Voyage AI and Jina AI)</ref>; unsupervised classification with EGA and prime-weight encoding; supervised classification heads; prompted classification with generative LLMs served by Groq, including strict JSON Schema outputs, ensembles, self-consistency, and LLM-as-judge; retrieval-augmented generation (RAG; <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Lewis et al., 2020)</ref> and topic discovery; Jev-based classification; do-it-yourself Jev-like classifiers; and a set of tools for calibration and uncertainty quantification.

text.text: The package relies on EGAnet (Golino & Christensen, 2026) for network estimation, on glmnet (Friedman, Hastie, & Tibshirani, 2010) for penalized regression, on reticulate (Kalinowski, Ushey, Allaire, & Tang, 2026) for local transformer models (Paszke et al., 2019; Wolf et al., 2020), and on httr2 (Wickham, 2026) for the APIs that do not require Python.
text.formatted: The package relies on EGAnet <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Golino & Christensen, 2026)</ref> for network estimation, on glmnet <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Friedman, Hastie, & Tibshirani, 2010)</ref> for penalized regression, on reticulate <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Kalinowski, Ushey, Allaire, & Tang, 2026)</ref> for local transformer models <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">(Paszke et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b117">Wolf et al., 2020)</ref>, and on httr2 <ref type="bibr" target="#b115">(Wickham, 2026)</ref> for the APIs that do not require Python.

text.text: The present paper is both a description of the software and a tutorial on the methods, written to dissect a set of questions that, in the experience of the author, recur whenever LLMs are used to classify text in psychological research: whether unsupervised network methods recover known categories from the embeddings of local and commercial models, and how the layers of a transformer can be combined (Section ); how much supervised classification heads gain over unsupervised methods when labels are available (Section ); how prompted LLMs should be engineered for classification (Section ); how topics can be discovered automatically, or with a human in the loop, when the categories are unknown (Section ); how a general-purpose classifier such as Jev is used, and how a Jev-like classifier can be built from local or API embeddings (Sections and ); what temperature scaling does, and does not do, to the probabilities of an LLM-based classifier (Section ); how uncertainty can be quantified, calibrated, and certified with conformal prediction (Section ); and how the reliability of the labels limits what any of these classifiers can be shown to achieve (Section ).
text.formatted: The present paper is both a description of the software and a tutorial on the methods, written to dissect a set of questions that, in the experience of the author, recur whenever LLMs are used to classify text in psychological research: whether unsupervised network methods recover known categories from the embeddings of local and commercial models, and how the layers of a transformer can be combined (Section ); how much supervised classification heads gain over unsupervised methods when labels are available (Section ); how prompted LLMs should be engineered for classification (Section ); how topics can be discovered automatically, or with a human in the loop, when the categories are unknown (Section ); how a general-purpose classifier such as Jev is used, and how a Jev-like classifier can be built from local or API embeddings <ref type="bibr">(Sections and )</ref>; what temperature scaling does, and does not do, to the probabilities of an LLM-based classifier (Section ); how uncertainty can be quantified, calibrated, and certified with conformal prediction (Section ); and how the reliability of the labels limits what any of these classifiers can be shown to achieve (Section ).

text.text: Every analysis uses three kinds of data: synthetic texts generated by LLMs, which were used in the course and ship with the package; descriptions of emotional situations from EmpatheticDialogues (Rashkin, Smith, Li, & Boureau, 2019), labeled with the emotion their writers chose, whose emotions mirror those of one of the synthetic data sets; and Reddit comments from GoEmotions (Demszky et al., 2020) with the same emotions, labeled by several raters who read each comment out of context.
text.formatted: Every analysis uses three kinds of data: synthetic texts generated by LLMs, which were used in the course and ship with the package; descriptions of emotional situations from EmpatheticDialogues <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">(Rashkin, Smith, Li, & Boureau, 2019)</ref>, labeled with the emotion their writers chose, whose emotions mirror those of one of the synthetic data sets; and Reddit comments from GoEmotions <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Demszky et al., 2020)</ref> with the same emotions, labeled by several raters who read each comment out of context.

text.text: The contrast between the three kinds of data turns out to be one of the main lessons of the paper: methods that look nearly perfect on synthetic texts lose part of their accuracy on real situations and much more of it on rater-labeled comments, where the agreement between raters, rather than the classifier, becomes the limiting factor.
Several R packages support parts of the workflow described here.

The tm (Feinerer et al., 2008), quanteda (Benoit et al., 2018), and tidytext (Silge & Robinson, 2016) packages provide infrastructure for bag-of-words text mining; topicmodels (Grün & Hornik, 2011) and stm (Roberts, Stewart, & Tingley, 2019) implement probabilistic topic models such as latent Dirichlet allocation (Blei, Ng, & Jordan, 2003); and the text package (O. Kjell, Giorgi, & Schwartz, 2023) gives R users access to transformer embeddings, with functions to train and evaluate supervised models on them and to visualize semantic differences between groups, building on a line of work that showed that language-based assessments can approach the reliability of rating scales (O. N. E. Kjell et al., 2019; O. N. E. Kjell, Sikström, Kjell, & Schwartz, 2022).
text.formatted: The tm <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Feinerer et al., 2008)</ref>, quanteda <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Benoit et al., 2018)</ref>, and tidytext <ref type="bibr" target="#b98">(Silge & Robinson, 2016)</ref> packages provide infrastructure for bag-of-words text mining; topicmodels <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Grün & Hornik, 2011)</ref> and stm <ref type="bibr" target="#b89">(Roberts, Stewart, & Tingley, 2019)</ref> implement probabilistic topic models such as latent Dirichlet allocation <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Blei, Ng, & Jordan, 2003)</ref>; and the text package (O. <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Kjell, Giorgi, & Schwartz, 2023)</ref> gives R users access to transformer embeddings, with functions to train and evaluate supervised models on them and to visualize semantic differences between groups, building on a line of work that showed that language-based assessments can approach the reliability of rating scales (O. N. E. <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Kjell et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">O.</ref> N. E. <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Kjell, Sikström, Kjell, & Schwartz, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: In Python, the transformers library (Wolf et al., 2020) and sentence encoders (Reimers & Gurevych, 2019) are the standard tools for embeddings, SetFit (Tunstall et al., 2022) trains few-shot classifiers on sentence embeddings, BERTopic (Grootendorst, 2022) clusters embeddings to discover topics, and TopicGPT (Pham, Hoyle, Sun, Resnik, & Iyyer, 2024) uses prompted LLMs for the same purpose.
text.formatted: In Python, the transformers library <ref type="bibr" target="#b117">(Wolf et al., 2020)</ref> and sentence encoders <ref type="bibr" target="#b88">(Reimers & Gurevych, 2019)</ref> are the standard tools for embeddings, SetFit <ref type="bibr" target="#b103">(Tunstall et al., 2022)</ref> trains few-shot classifiers on sentence embeddings, BERTopic <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Grootendorst, 2022)</ref> clusters embeddings to discover topics, and TopicGPT <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">(Pham, Hoyle, Sun, Resnik, & Iyyer, 2024)</ref> uses prompted LLMs for the same purpose.

text.text: Table 1 summarizes how llmClassificR complements these tools.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref> summarizes how llmClassificR complements these tools.

text.text: Its distinctive features are the integration of network psychometrics with embeddings from many sources (including the multiplex prime-weight encoding of transformer layers), the coverage of the three families of LLM-based classifiers available in 2026 (prompted generative models, embedding-based classifiers, and Jev) under the same output format, and the inclusion of calibration and conformal prediction as first-class steps of the classification workflow, rather than as optional diagnostics.
This section describes, as briefly as possible, the methods that the package implements, using a common notation.
A corpus contains n texts, each assigned (when t , which is what the function embed_local() returns for every layer of any model available in the Hugging Face hub.
Decoder LLMs, such as the Qwen2.5 family (Qwen et al., 2024), can be used in the same way, and their mean-pooled hidden states will be called LLM embeddings in the present paper.
text.formatted: Decoder LLMs, such as the Qwen2.5 family <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">(Qwen et al., 2024)</ref>, can be used in the same way, and their mean-pooled hidden states will be called LLM embeddings in the present paper.

text.text: Layers differ in what they encode: lower layers are closer to the surface form of the text, middle layers capture syntactic and semantic relations, and upper layers specialize in the pre-training objective (Jawahar et al., 2019; Rogers et al., 2020; Tenney et al., 2019), while raw contextual embeddings occupy a narrow cone of the vector space, which makes all cosine similarities large (Ethayarajh, 2019).
text.formatted: Layers differ in what they encode: lower layers are closer to the surface form of the text, middle layers capture syntactic and semantic relations, and upper layers specialize in the pre-training objective <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Jawahar et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b90">Rogers et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b101">Tenney et al., 2019)</ref>, while raw contextual embeddings occupy a narrow cone of the vector space, which makes all cosine similarities large <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Ethayarajh, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Sentence encoders, such as all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (Reimers & Gurevych, 2019; W. Wang et al., 2020) and all-mpnet-base-v2 (Reimers & Gurevych, 2019; Song, Tan, Qin, Lu, & Liu, 2020), are trained with contrastive objectives so that cosine similarities between texts reflect similarity in meaning, and are available in the package through embed_sentences().

Wang et al., 2020)</ref> and all-mpnet-base-v2 <ref type="bibr" target="#b88">(Reimers & Gurevych, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b99">Song, Tan, Qin, Lu, & Liu, 2020)</ref>, are trained with contrastive objectives so that cosine similarities between texts reflect similarity in meaning, and are available in the package through embed_sentences().

text.text: Commercial embedding services such as Voyage AI (Voyage AI, 2026) and Jina AI (Sturua et al., 2024), available through embed_voyage() and embed_jina(), follow the same principle with much larger models, and some of them are trained with Matryoshka representation learning, so that the first dimensions of a vector form a useful lower-dimensional embedding (Kusupati et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Commercial embedding services such as Voyage AI <ref type="bibr" target="#b109">(Voyage AI, 2026)</ref> and Jina AI <ref type="bibr" target="#b100">(Sturua et al., 2024)</ref>, available through embed_voyage() and embed_jina(), follow the same principle with much larger models, and some of them are trained with Matryoshka representation learning, so that the first dimensions of a vector form a useful lower-dimensional embedding <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(Kusupati et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The quality of embedding models is typically compared with large benchmarks (Muennighoff, Tazi, Magne, & Reimers, 2023), but their behavior on psychological constructs needs to be checked on the data at hand, which is one of the goals of the present tutorial.
text.formatted: The quality of embedding models is typically compared with large benchmarks <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">(Muennighoff, Tazi, Magne, & Reimers, 2023)</ref>, but their behavior on psychological constructs needs to be checked on the data at hand, which is one of the goals of the present tutorial.

text.text: EGA estimates the number and composition of dimensions in multivariate data by modeling the variables as nodes of a network and detecting the communities of densely connected nodes (Golino & Epskamp, 2017; Golino et al., 2020).
text.formatted: EGA estimates the number and composition of dimensions in multivariate data by modeling the variables as nodes of a network and detecting the communities of densely connected nodes <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Golino & Epskamp, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Golino et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: To classify texts without labels, the roles of rows and columns are swapped: each text is a node, the p embedding dimensions play the role of observations, and the edge between two texts reflects how strongly their embedding vectors co-vary across dimensions.

In llmClassificR, ega_classify() estimates the network with the triangulated maximally filtered graph (TMFG; Massara, Di Matteo, & Aste, 2017), which retains 3n -6 edges, chosen greedily to maximize the sum of the retained correlations under the constraint that the graph remains planar, and detects communities with the walktrap algorithm (Pons & Latapy, 2006), which merges nodes that are close in terms of short random walks on the network (Fortunato, 2010).
text.formatted: In llmClassificR, ega_classify() estimates the network with the triangulated maximally filtered graph (TMFG; <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Massara, Di Matteo, & Aste, 2017)</ref>, which retains 3n -6 edges, chosen greedily to maximize the sum of the retained correlations under the constraint that the graph remains planar, and detects communities with the walktrap algorithm <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">(Pons & Latapy, 2006)</ref>, which merges nodes that are close in terms of short random walks on the network <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Fortunato, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: The number of steps of the random walks controls the granularity of the solution, and the function EGA.fit() of EGAnet chooses it by minimizing the total entropy fit index (TEFI; Golino et al., 2021), an information-theoretic fit measure that does not use the labels.
text.formatted: The number of steps of the random walks controls the granularity of the solution, and the function EGA.fit() of EGAnet chooses it by minimizing the total entropy fit index (TEFI; <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Golino et al., 2021)</ref>, an information-theoretic fit measure that does not use the labels.

text.text: Each community is a candidate category, and texts that EGA cannot assign to any community are left unclassified.
Running EGA on each layer of a transformer produces L + 1 networks defined on the same n texts, that is, a multiplex network.

Averaging or concatenating the layers before estimating a single network is one way of using all of them, but it mixes the representations before the networks are estimated. Santoro and Nicosia (2020) proposed an encoding of multiplex networks in which each layer receives a distinct prime number, and Golino et al. (2025) adapted it to psychological networks in the ergodicity information index.

(2025)</ref> adapted it to psychological networks in the ergodicity information index.

text.text: The function prime_weight_encode() applies this idea to texts.

Let a (k) ij be the weight of the edge between texts i and j in the network of layer (or source) k = 1, . . . , M , and p k the k-th prime number (2, 3, 5, 7, . . . ), assigned after ordering the networks by their number of edges; since every TMFG network on n texts has 3n -6 edges, the primes follow the order of the layers, so that the upper layers of an encoder receive the largest primes.
The encoding of the pair (i, j) is which combines the information of all layers in a single matrix, and walktrap is then applied to X for each number of steps between 2 and 25.
The solution reported by the package is chosen without labels, as the first number of steps that produces the most frequent number of communities across the 24 solutions.

A property of Equation (1) that matters in practice is that a network that does not link texts i and j still contributes p 0 k = 1, so that a pair never linked in any layer receives X ij = M , the floor of the encoding, and the diagonal (where every a
Since walktrap is a random walk on the weighted network, the floor acts as a constant edge between every pair of texts, through which part of every step jumps to an arbitrary text.

Version 0.2.2 of the package therefore also returns the floor-free network which is the share of the largest possible linkage of the pair (0 for pairs never linked, 1 for pairs linked with weight 1 in every layer).

Rescaling alone does not change walktrap, which is invariant to a common multiplier of the edge weights, but removing the floor does; the argument remove_floor = TRUE runs walktrap on R, while the default keeps the original encoding.
The floor-free network is always used to visualize the encoding with plot_prime_weight(), because the original encoding would draw an edge between every pair of texts.
Section works through the encoding step by step, on a toy example and on the layers of BERT.

When labels are available, the partition found without them can be compared with the true classes with the normalized mutual information (NMI; Danon, Díaz-Guilera, Duch, & Arenas, 2005; Vinh, Epps, & Bailey, 2010), which is 1 when the partition reproduces the classes exactly and close to 0 when it is unrelated to them, and which does not require the communities to be named or to be as many as the classes.
text.formatted: When labels are available, the partition found without them can be compared with the true classes with the normalized mutual information (NMI; <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Danon, Díaz-Guilera, Duch, & Arenas, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b107">Vinh, Epps, & Bailey, 2010)</ref>, which is 1 when the partition reproduces the classes exactly and close to 0 when it is unrelated to them, and which does not require the communities to be named or to be as many as the classes.

text.text: The package computes NMI = I(Y ; C)/ max{H(Y ), H(C)}, where I(Y ; C) is the mutual information between the classes Y and the communities C and H denotes entropy, which is the most conservative of the usual normalizations (Vinh et al., 2010); the arithmetic-mean normalization of Danon et al. (2005) is available through the argument variant of compute_nmi().

(2005)</ref> is available through the argument variant of compute_nmi().

text.text: The function match_communities() does this with the Hungarian algorithm (Kuhn, 1955), as implemented in clue (Hornik, 2005), which assigns a different class to each community so that the number of texts whose community is named after their own class is as large as possible; communities left over when there are more communities than classes are named "Extra 1", "Extra 2", and so on, and their texts count as errors.

text.text: The labels are used only after the communities were found, so the resulting matched accuracy is a legitimate summary of an unsupervised solution, but choosing the number of walktrap steps with the highest NMI is not, because it selects the solution with the labels; the package reports such values as optimistic diagnostics only.
Confidence intervals for accuracies are computed with the exact binomial method (Clopper & Pearson, 1934).

text.text: When labeled texts are available, a classification head is a small model fitted on top of frozen embeddings, in the spirit of the linear probes used to study what each layer of a neural network encodes (Alain & Bengio, 2017; Hewitt & Liang, 2019).

text.text: The function cv_logistic() fits an elastic-net multinomial logistic regression (Friedman et al., 2010; Zou & Hastie, 2005) with stratified k-fold cross-validation, choosing the penalty within each training fold, so that every text is predicted by a model that never saw it (Bates, Hastie, & Tibshirani, 2024; Nadeau & Bengio, 2003); probe_layers() repeats this for every layer of an encoder, and learning_curve() estimates how accuracy grows with the number of labeled texts per class, which indicates whether collecting more labels is likely to pay off.

text.text: Generative LLMs classify texts when prompted with an instruction, the list of categories, and, optionally, a few labeled examples (few-shot prompting; Brown et al., 2020; Min et al., 2022) or a request to reason before answering (chain-of-thought; Wei et al., 2022; Kojima, Gu, Reid, Matsuo, & Iwasawa, 2022).
text.formatted: Generative LLMs classify texts when prompted with an instruction, the list of categories, and, optionally, a few labeled examples (few-shot prompting; <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Brown et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Min et al., 2022)</ref> or a request to reason before answering (chain-of-thought; <ref type="bibr" target="#b113">Wei et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Kojima, Gu, Reid, Matsuo, & Iwasawa, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Their answers are free text, which creates engineering problems that the package handles inside every classify_*() function: texts are sent in batches (40 per request by default) to control costs and rate limits, but batches are shuffled, since an ordered batch allows the model to exploit the sequence of labels rather than the content of each text (Lu et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2021); answers are mapped to the allowed classes with normalize_labels(), and anything else becomes a missing value counted as an error; and results are returned in the original order of the texts.

Wang et al., 2023), and a model can be asked to act as an expert judge that cites evidence for its decisions (LLM-as-judge; Zheng et al., 2023).

text.text: RAG retrieves the documents most similar to a query, usually by cosine similarity between embeddings, and asks an LLM to answer using only those documents as context (Lewis et al., 2020).
text.formatted: RAG retrieves the documents most similar to a query, usually by cosine similarity between embeddings, and asks an LLM to answer using only those documents as context <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Lewis et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: In llmClassificR, retrieve_similar() and rag_generate() implement the two steps, discover_topics() asks for a fixed number of topics (each with a label and a description) grounded in representative documents, and classify_with_rag() chains embedding, topic discovery, and classification of every text into the discovered topics.

The same goal can be pursued with a human in the loop and without generative models: EGA finds the communities, the most typical words of each community (those whose share of texts in the community most exceeds their share of the other texts) are listed, the most central texts of each community are read by the analyst, and the analyst's names and descriptions of the communities define a zero-shot classifier (next subsection).
This human-guided route is related to embedding-based topic models such as BERTopic (Grootendorst, 2022), and its LLM-based counterpart to TopicGPT (Pham et al., 2024).
text.formatted: This human-guided route is related to embedding-based topic models such as BERTopic <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Grootendorst, 2022)</ref>, and its LLM-based counterpart to TopicGPT <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">(Pham et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Jev answers three types of typed questions about a text (TypeSafe, 2026): a Choice question picks one of up to 255 options and returns a probability for each option, a Noul question returns the probability that a yes/no statement is true (so that several Noul questions about the same text form a multi-label classifier whose probabilities need not sum to 1), and a Score question rates the text on an ordinal rubric with 2 to 10 levels and returns the probability-weighted level.
Each question has instructions and criteria, the descriptions of when each option applies, which play the role of the items of a measurement instrument.

The architecture, training algorithm, and training data of Jev have not been disclosed; according to its developers, as reported by Raschka (2026), the model was trained only on curated synthetic data with a proprietary procedure called reinforcement learning for calibrated decisions, and its documentation describes its probabilities as well calibrated.
text.formatted: The architecture, training algorithm, and training data of Jev have not been disclosed; according to its developers, as reported by <ref type="bibr" target="#b84">Raschka (2026)</ref>, the model was trained only on curated synthetic data with a proprietary procedure called reinforcement learning for calibrated decisions, and its documentation describes its probabilities as well calibrated.

text.text: Raschka (2026) sketched how a classifier of this kind could work.

A transformer reads the text together with each candidate option c and produces a vector h c per candidate, a shared head computes a score s c = w ⊤ h c + b, and a softmax over the candidates turns the scores into probabilities.
Because w and b are shared, the number of candidates can change from task to task without retraining, and the bias b cancels in the softmax (it matters only for yes/no questions).

The package implements a bi-encoder version of this idea that runs on a laptop: text i and the description of class c are embedded separately, with any of the embedding functions, and their cosine similarity s ic is the score, a strategy known as dataless classification (Chang, Ratinov, Roth, & Srikumar, 2008) and related to entailment-based zero-shot classification (Yin, Hay, & Roth, 2019).
text.formatted: The package implements a bi-encoder version of this idea that runs on a laptop: text i and the description of class c are embedded separately, with any of the embedding functions, and their cosine similarity s ic is the score, a strategy known as dataless classification <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Chang, Ratinov, Roth, & Srikumar, 2008)</ref> and related to entailment-based zero-shot classification <ref type="bibr" target="#b120">(Yin, Hay, & Roth, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: The function classify_by_description() returns softmax(s ic /T ) with a temperature T , which is equivalent to a head w whose elements all equal 1/T applied to h ic = x i ⊙ d c (the element-wise product of the unit-length text and description embeddings), and train_shared_head() learns w from labeled tasks to test whether such a head transfers to tasks with new labels.

The difference from the classifier sketched by Raschka (2026) is that a bi-encoder never reads the text and the description together, while a cross-encoder does, which usually improves accuracy at a higher computational cost (Humeau, Shuster, Lachaux, & Weston, 2020).

text.text: A classifier is calibrated when, among the texts to which it assigns confidence q (the largest probability), the proportion classified correctly is close to q (Guo et al., 2017).
text.formatted: A classifier is calibrated when, among the texts to which it assigns confidence q (the largest probability), the proportion classified correctly is close to q <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Guo et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: The package reports the expected calibration error (ECE; Pakdaman Naeini, Cooper, & Hauskrecht, 2015), which averages the absolute gap between accuracy and confidence across 10 confidence bins weighted by their number of texts; the Brier score (Brier, 1950), the mean squared distance between the probability vector and the one-hot vector of the true class; and the negative log-likelihood (NLL) of the true class.
text.formatted: The package reports the expected calibration error (ECE; Pakdaman Naeini, Cooper, & Hauskrecht, 2015), which averages the absolute gap between accuracy and confidence across 10 confidence bins weighted by their number of texts; the Brier score <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Brier, 1950)</ref>, the mean squared distance between the probability vector and the one-hot vector of the true class; and the negative log-likelihood (NLL) of the true class.

text.text: The Brier score and the NLL are strictly proper scoring rules, which means that their expected value is optimized only by the true probabilities (Gneiting & Raftery, 2007), a property that recent work exploited to train reasoning models to state calibrated confidences with the reward c -(q -c) 2 , where c indicates a correct answer (Damani et al., 2026); the function rlcr_reward() implements this reward for teaching purposes.

text.text: Reliability diagrams (reliability_table() and plot_reliability()) display accuracy against confidence by bin.

Temperature scaling divides the scores (logits) by a single positive number T before the softmax, with T chosen to minimize the NLL on a calibration set (Guo et al., 2017; Hinton, Vinyals, & Dean, 2015); since all scores are divided by the same number, the ranking of the classes, and therefore the accuracy, does not change, and only the confidence is repaired (T > 1 softens over-confident probabilities, T < 1 sharpens under-confident ones).
text.formatted: Temperature scaling divides the scores (logits) by a single positive number T before the softmax, with T chosen to minimize the NLL on a calibration set <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Guo et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Hinton, Vinyals, & Dean, 2015)</ref>; since all scores are divided by the same number, the ranking of the classes, and therefore the accuracy, does not change, and only the confidence is repaired (T > 1 softens over-confident probabilities, T < 1 sharpens under-confident ones).

text.text: This post hoc temperature must not be confused with the sampling temperature of generative LLMs, which controls the randomness of the generated tokens (Holtzman, Buys, Du, Forbes, & Choi, 2020) and affects classification only indirectly, for example through the diversity of the votes in self-consistency.
text.formatted: This post hoc temperature must not be confused with the sampling temperature of generative LLMs, which controls the randomness of the generated tokens <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Holtzman, Buys, Du, Forbes, & Choi, 2020)</ref> and affects classification only indirectly, for example through the diversity of the votes in self-consistency.

text.text: Platt scaling fits p = logit -1 (as + b) to the score s of a binary question (Platt, 2000) and is the natural method for yes/no (Noul-like) questions, where the bias matters; richer alternatives exist (Kull et al., 2019).

text.text: Calibration is not the only aspect of uncertainty: selective classification lets a classifier abstain on the texts it is least confident about, trading coverage for accuracy (Geifman & El-Yaniv, 2017), and split conformal prediction turns any probabilistic classifier into a set-valued classifier with a finite-sample guarantee (Angelopoulos & Bates, 2023; Vovk et al., 2005).
text.formatted: Calibration is not the only aspect of uncertainty: selective classification lets a classifier abstain on the texts it is least confident about, trading coverage for accuracy <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Geifman & El-Yaniv, 2017)</ref>, and split conformal prediction turns any probabilistic classifier into a set-valued classifier with a finite-sample guarantee <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Angelopoulos & Bates, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b108">Vovk et al., 2005)</ref>.

text.text: With a calibration set of size n c and nonconformity scores e i = 1 -pi,y i (one minus the probability of the true class), the threshold q is the ⌈(n c + 1)(1 -α)⌉-th smallest score, and the prediction set of a new text contains every class c with pc ≥ 1 -q (Sadinle, Lei, & Wasserman, 2019).
text.formatted: With a calibration set of size n c and nonconformity scores e i = 1 -pi,y i (one minus the probability of the true class), the threshold q is the ⌈(n c + 1)(1 -α)⌉-th smallest score, and the prediction set of a new text contains every class c with pc ≥ 1 -q <ref type="bibr" target="#b92">(Sadinle, Lei, & Wasserman, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: If the calibration and new texts are exchangeable, the set contains the true class with probability at least 1 -α, whatever the classifier, and set sizes become a direct, interpretable measure of uncertainty (Kumar et al., 2023; Quach et al., 2024; Romano, Sesia, & Candès, 2020).
text.formatted: If the calibration and new texts are exchangeable, the set contains the true class with probability at least 1 -α, whatever the classifier, and set sizes become a direct, interpretable measure of uncertainty <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(Kumar et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">Quach et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b91">Romano, Sesia, & Candès, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: In the present paper, this distribution-free guarantee is what is meant by certification, and its main assumption, exchangeability between calibration and new texts, is precisely what is violated when a model calibrated on synthetic texts is applied to real ones.

The llmClassificR package Installation and setup The package is installed from GitHub; the functions that run local transformer models use Python through reticulate, in an environment created once with the uv package manager, while the functions that call Groq (generative models), TypeSafe (Jev), and Jina AI are written in pure R with httr2, and the Voyage AI functions use the official Python client. install.packages("remotes") remotes::install_github("hfgolino/llmClassificR") library("llmClassificR") setup_llm_env() # once: creates the Python environment "llm_env" with uv activate_llm_env() # at the start of every session, before other packages verify_setup(test_apis = TRUE)
API keys are never written in scripts: each key is stored once in the user's ~/.
Renviron file (for example, the line GROQ_API_KEY=...), and set_groq_key(), set_voyage_key(), set_jina_key(), and set_typesafe_key() read them from there.
Two practical details are handled by the setup functions.

First, activate_llm_env() loads PyTorch at the beginning of the session, because native libraries loaded later by other packages can clash with those shipped with PyTorch; second, embed_local() runs, by default, in a separate background R process created with callr (Csárdi & Chang, 2026), so that a crash of the Python runtime becomes an ordinary R error instead of terminating the user's session.
text.formatted: First, activate_llm_env() loads PyTorch at the beginning of the session, because native libraries loaded later by other packages can clash with those shipped with PyTorch; second, embed_local() runs, by default, in a separate background R process created with callr <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Csárdi & Chang, 2026)</ref>, so that a crash of the Python runtime becomes an ordinary R error instead of terminating the user's session.

text.text: Four principles guided the design of the package.

The first is one function per step: each step of the workflows described in Section corresponds to one function with a small number of arguments and sensible defaults, so that a complete analysis reads as a sequence of named steps (Table 2).
text.formatted: The first is one function per step: each step of the workflows described in Section corresponds to one function with a small number of arguments and sensible defaults, so that a complete analysis reads as a sequence of named steps (Table <ref type="table">2</ref>).

text.text: The second is a common output format: every classifier returns a data frame with one row per text, in the original order, containing the predicted class (prediction), the confidence, and, when the method produces them, one column of probabilities per class, so that evaluate_classification(), calibration_metrics(), reliability_table(), and compare_methods() accept the output of any classifier, from a bag-of-words baseline to Jev.

The third is explicit treatment of failures: invalid or missing answers are returned as NA and counted as errors (and reported in the column n_invalid), never silently replaced by a class, and texts that EGA does not assign to any community are treated as singleton clusters when the NMI is computed.

The fourth is reproducibility: random operations (folds, shuffling, layouts) take a seed argument and restore the global random state afterwards, API functions retry rate-limited requests with exponential backoff, and Jev functions report the tokens used and their cost with jev_usage().

The package ships seven data sets, five of which are corpora of short texts used throughout the course: extraversion, extraversion_3p, and extraversion_llama each contain 120 descriptions of four facets of extraversion, 30 per facet (Friendly, Positive, Assertive, and Energetic), resembling facets of the IPIP-NEO and NEO PI-R (Costa & McCrae, 1992; Johnson, 2014), written by three different LLMs (gpt-oss-20b in the first person, gpt-oss-120b in the third person, and llama-3.1-8b); neuroticism contains 120 first-person texts expressing four emotional states, 30 per state (Sad, Excited, Angry, and Friendly); and personality_descriptions contains 110 social-media-style bios, 22 for each Big Five trait (Goldberg, 1993).

text.text: The other two data sets are label_descriptions, with one description per class for three tasks (the four extraversion facets, the four emotions, and the Big Five), and minilm_embeddings, with pre-computed sentence embeddings of all texts and descriptions, which allow the Jev-like and calibration examples to run without Python or API keys.

Three synthetic corpora are used in most illustrations, namely the Big Five bios, the first-person extraversion facets, and the emotion texts (data sets personality_descriptions, extraversion, and neuroticism); the two other extraversion corpora are used to study transfer across generators and to train Jev-like heads.
Two real corpora complement them, and they were chosen because they differ in who decided the label of each text, a difference that turns out to matter as much as the classifier.

The first real corpus comes from EmpatheticDialogues (Rashkin et al., 2019), a data set of 24,850 conversations, each grounded in a short situation that a crowdworker described after selecting an emotion word, writing, in one to three sentences, about a situation in which they had felt that way.
text.formatted: The first real corpus comes from EmpatheticDialogues <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">(Rashkin et al., 2019)</ref>, a data set of 24,850 conversations, each grounded in a short situation that a crowdworker described after selecting an emotion word, writing, in one to three sentences, about a situation in which they had felt that way.

text.text: The label of a situation is therefore the emotion its writer intended to convey, much as the label of a synthetic text is the category the LLM was asked to write about, with the difference that the writers are people describing events of their own lives.
Four of its 32 emotions mirror those of the synthetic neuroticism corpus: angry (Angry), sad (Sad), excited (Excited), and caring (Friendly, the least exact correspondence).

From the situations labeled with these four emotions (the data set is distributed under the CC BY-NC 4.0 license), exact duplicates and situations with fewer than 4 or more than 60 words were removed, and 150 situations were sampled at random for each emotion, giving 600 situations (median length 15 words) that were split, within each emotion, into a calibration half and a test half (300 situations each).
These situations are the real texts of every illustration that follows.

The second real corpus is GoEmotions (Demszky et al., 2020), about 58,000 English Reddit comments annotated with any number of 27 emotion categories (or neutral) by several raters, whose rater-level annotations are public (the documentation of the data set lists the Apache License 2.0).
text.formatted: The second real corpus is GoEmotions <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Demszky et al., 2020)</ref>, about 58,000 English Reddit comments annotated with any number of 27 emotion categories (or neutral) by several raters, whose rater-level annotations are public (the documentation of the data set lists the Apache License 2.0).

text.text: Here the label is not chosen by the writer but inferred by raters who read the comment without its context, and the agreement between raters is limited.

A subset with the same four emotions (anger, sadness, excitement, and caring) was built with the aggregation rule of the original corpus: after removing ratings flagged as very unclear, a comment was eligible when at least three raters annotated it and exactly one of the 28 categories was chosen by at least two raters, that category being one of the four target emotions, and when it had between 4 and 60 words; 150 eligible comments were then sampled at random for each emotion, and the 600 comments were split in the same way as the situations.

The median proportion of raters who chose the gold emotion of a comment is 0.67, only 20% of the comments were labeled unanimously, and 34% of the individual ratings include none of the four emotions; an informal audit of 1,000

GoEmotions comments by a data-labeling company judged about 30% of the original labels to be seriously wrong, attributing the errors mainly to the absence of context and to the raters' unfamiliarity with the slang and culture of the comments (Chen, 2022).
text.formatted: GoEmotions comments by a data-labeling company judged about 30% of the original labels to be seriously wrong, attributing the errors mainly to the absence of context and to the raters' unfamiliarity with the slang and culture of the comments <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Chen, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: GoEmotions is used in Section to show how the reliability of the labels limits the accuracy that any classifier can reach, and why the probabilities of a classifier trained on majority labels say little about human disagreement.
Both subsets and the code used to build them are part of the replication materials.

Texts written for a given category, whether by an LLM or by a person asked to describe an emotion, share more of their vocabulary within a label than comments labeled after the fact: the within-label overlap ranges from 0.068 to 0.116 in the synthetic corpora, is 0.084 in the EmpatheticDialogues situations, and only 0.035 in the GoEmotions comments, and the most frequent three-word opening starts up to 6.7% of the synthetic texts against 1.7% of the situations and 0.5% of the comments (Table 3), the repetitiveness of synthetic texts being a well-documented property of text generated by LLMs (Long et al., 2024; Shumailov et al., 2024).

Section compares this curve with those of classifiers built on embeddings.
The first question of a classification study does not need labels: do the texts form communities, and do the communities correspond to the categories of interest?
The replication script answers it, for each corpus and for each encoder with access to its layers (BERT, ModernBERT, and the decoder LLM Qwen2.5-0.5B), with five label-free solutions:

EGA on the average of the layers, EGA.fit() on the same average (walktrap steps chosen by TEFI), EGA on the concatenated layers, and the prime-weight encoding of the per-layer networks, with and without the floor.

text.text: On the synthetic corpora, the prime-weight encoding of the BERT layers was the best single-encoder solution: it recovered the five traits of the Big Five bios with a matched accuracy of 92.7% (NMI = 0.854, 5 communities) and the four extraversion facets with 95.0%, compared with 82.7% and 85.0% for EGA on the concatenated layers and 66.4% and 81.7% for EGA on the averaged layers, and adding the two sentence encoders to the BERT layers as two more networks gave similar results (91.8% and 95.8%).

Combining the networks of the layers, rather than combining the layers before estimating a network, preserves the information that each layer contributes, which is what the multiplex view of Section suggests, and the next subsection opens the encoding to show where this information comes from.

The encoders differed sharply: the raw layers of ModernBERT, which achieves state-of-the-art accuracy after fine-tuning (Warner et al., 2025), produced almost no trait structure without labels (NMI between 0.03 and 0.11 across the five solutions for the bios), and the decoder LLM fell between the two encoders, with the floor-free encoding clearly better than the original one for the bios (89.1% against 77.3%), while the original encoding was better for BERT (92.7% against 72.7%).
text.formatted: The encoders differed sharply: the raw layers of ModernBERT, which achieves state-of-the-art accuracy after fine-tuning <ref type="bibr" target="#b112">(Warner et al., 2025)</ref>, produced almost no trait structure without labels (NMI between 0.03 and 0.11 across the five solutions for the bios), and the decoder LLM fell between the two encoders, with the floor-free encoding clearly better than the original one for the bios (89.1% against 77.3%), while the original encoding was better for BERT (92.7% against 72.7%).

text.text: This mixed pattern agrees with the comparison reported in the documentation of prime_weight_encode(), and is the reason why the floor-free variant is an option rather than the default.
On the real situations, no label-free solution recovered the four emotions as cleanly, but the emotions were clearly present in the structure of the texts.

The prime-weight encoding of the BERT layers reached the highest matched accuracy of all label-free solutions, 54.2% with only 3 communities (NMI = 0.244), against 34.5% and 28.2% for EGA on the averaged and concatenated layers, while EGA on the MPNet sentence embeddings found 15 communities with the highest NMI (0.308) but a lower matched accuracy (39.2%).

The two summaries answer different questions: the NMI measures how much a partition says about the emotions, whatever its number of communities, while the matched accuracy measures how well it could serve as a classifier, so that a partition with many communities is penalized (only four of them can be named after an emotion, and the texts of the others count as errors), and a partition with fewer communities than emotions cannot classify one of the emotions at all.

Adding the two sentence encoders to the BERT layers, which helped on the synthetic corpora, collapsed the encoding of the situations into 2 communities (NMI = 0.008), a reminder that a multiplex encoding is not guaranteed to improve with more sources.

As Section shows, the communities of the situations correspond to recurrent kinds of situations, most of which are typical of one emotion, so that emotion is one of the organizing principles of these texts, but not the only one.
The prime-weight encoding is easier to understand on a toy example before it is applied to real layers.

Consider three networks (layers) defined on the same four texts, in which texts A and B are linked in every layer, texts C and D are linked in every layer, B and C are linked only in the first layer, A and C only in the second, and A and D in none; each layer receives a prime number, and each pair receives the sum of the primes raised to the weights of its edges (Equation ( 1)):  Walktrap is then applied to the encoded network for 2 to 25 steps.

text.text: Without labels, the package chooses the first number of steps that produces the most frequent number of communities across the 24 solutions, 5 steps for the original encoding (5 communities) and 2 steps for the floor-free network (7 communities); the NMI with the true traits, computed for every number of steps, is a diagnostic that uses the labels and is not used to choose the solution (Figure 3, bottom).

text.text: For these bios, the original encoding chose 5 communities at 5 steps, a solution whose NMI (0.854) is the highest of the 24 solutions, while the floor-free network chose 7 communities at 2 steps (NMI = 0.702), although its solutions with 6 communities, which appear from 16 steps on, agree more with the traits (NMI up to 0.794).
The selection rule does not use the labels, and its choice is therefore not always the solution closest to the traits, which is the price of an honest unsupervised analysis.

text.text: For the Big Five bios, EGA.fit() on the Voyage AI and Jina AI embeddings reached matched accuracies of 75.5% and 73.6%, above both sentence encoders but well below the prime-weight encoding of the BERT layers (92.7%), and adding either service to the 13 layers of BERT as one more network gave 91.8% and 90.0%, so that the commercial representations added nothing to what the layers of a small local encoder already contained.

For the situations, EGA on the Voyage AI embeddings found 15 communities with an NMI of 0.307, about the same as with MPNet, but left 291 of the 600 situations outside any community, which is why its matched accuracy was only 41.5%; the prime-weight encodings of the BERT layers together with Voyage AI or Jina AI found 4 communities each, with matched accuracies of 54.0% and 55.8%, the latter being the highest of any label-free solution in the paper, but only 1.6 points above the BERT layers alone.

Larger models, in other words, did not make the emotions the dominant structure of the situations, and, as the following sections show, the advantage of the commercial embeddings appears only when labels are available, and, for Voyage AI, also when label descriptions are.
When labeled texts are available, the same embeddings can feed a supervised head.

The replication script fits a cross-validated head on eight representations of the EmpatheticDialogues situations: the bag-of-words features, the last layer and the average of the layers of BERT, the average of the ModernBERT layers, the last layer and the average of the layers of the decoder LLM Qwen2.5-0.5B, and the two sentence encoders. head_table[order(-head_table$accuracy), c("method", "accuracy", "macro_F1", "ECE")]
With labels, every representation classified the situations more accurately than any label-free method (Table 6).
text.formatted: With labels, every representation classified the situations more accurately than any label-free method (Table <ref type="table">6</ref>).

text.text: The best head on a local representation, the MPNet sentence embeddings, classified 83.3% of the situations correctly (95% CI 80.1% to 86.2%), followed by MiniLM (81.7%) and by the average of the layers of the decoder LLM (81.5%), while the bag-of-words baseline reached 64.8%.

The same head fitted on the embeddings of the two commercial services, with the code shown in Section , reached 87.2% with Voyage AI (95% CI 84.2% to 89.7%), the most accurate head of all, and 84.8% with Jina AI, so that the larger models that added nothing to the label-free solutions did make the emotions more linearly readable, by about 4 points in the case of Voyage AI, although its interval overlaps with that of the MPNet head.
Two details are worth noting.

Averaging the layers was better than using the last layer, for BERT (78.5% for the last layer against 79.8%) as well as for the LLM (78.2% against 81.5%), in line with the observation that the last layers of a model specialize in its pre-training objective (Rogers et al., 2020); and the confidence intervals of the heads on local embeddings overlap, so that, with 600 situations, the choice among them is a matter of convenience rather than of accuracy.

text.text: The ECE of the embedding-based heads ranged from 0.042 to 0.202, and the most accurate heads were not the best calibrated, a point taken up in Section.

text.text: Trained on the 120 synthetic emotion texts, the heads on MiniLM and MPNet classified 62.2% and 74.0% of the real situations correctly, far better than the 36.7% of the bag-of-words classifier trained on the same texts, because sentence embeddings abstract away from the exact words used by the generator; the MPNet head trained on synthetic texts was only 9.30 points less accurate than the head trained on real situations, which shows that synthetic texts can be useful training data when the representation generalizes, even if they are a poor guide to the accuracy of a method.
The confusion matrices of Figure 6 show where the errors lie.

The supervised MPNet head confused mostly anger with sadness (15 angry situations classified as sad and TEXT CLASSIFICATION WITH LLMCLASSIFICR 47 19 sad situations classified as angry) and caring with sadness (18 and 13), the zero-shot classifier confused sad situations with caring (25) and angry situations with sadness (23), and the bag-of-words head assigned 49 angry situations to sadness.

Situations in which something bad happens to the writer can describe anger as well as sadness, and situations about the misfortune of someone the writer cares for can describe caring as well as sadness, which is a property of emotional situations rather than of the classifiers.

The probes per layer, run with probe_layers(), show what each layer of an encoder or LLM makes linearly readable with labels, and can be set against the NMI of the EGA solution of the same layer, which shows what the layer organizes into communities without labels (Figure 7).

text.text: For the real situations, the heads read the emotions from every layer, with accuracies rising from the input embeddings to the middle and upper layers (between 69% and 80% for BERT and between 68% and 83% for the LLM, where the maxima are optimistic because they are chosen with the labels), while the NMI of the EGA communities of the same layers was at most 0.214.

The emotion is linearly readable in every layer, but it is only one of the factors that organize the representations, which is exactly the situation in which supervised heads, or the description-based classifiers of the following sections, are needed.

The prompted classifiers are evaluated on the 300 test situations, so that the calibration situations remain available to fit temperatures (Section ) and conformal thresholds (Section ), and two situations per emotion from the calibration half serve as few-shot examples.

text.text: The first sends the test situations sorted by their true emotion, in batches that preserve that order (shuffle = FALSE), which reproduces a common mistake in practice, since data files are often sorted by category; the comparison with the default (shuffled) batches estimates how much an LLM exploits the order of the texts instead of their content.

The second asks the same model five times at a sampling temperature of 0.8 and uses the share of votes as a probability (self-consistency), which is the only way to obtain probabilities from a provider that does not return token probabilities, other than asking the model to verbalize them (classify_scores()).

On the test situations, direct zero-shot prompting reached an accuracy of 86.3% (Table 7), few-shot prompting 87.0%, chain-of-thought 86.3%, the LLM-as-judge 86.7%, and the strict JSON Schema classifier, run with the smaller gpt-oss-20b, 87.7%; the ensemble of three models reached 87.3%, with the three models agreeing on 88% of the situations, and self-consistency, the majority of five answers sampled at a temperature of 0.8, was the most accurate prompted classifier, with 88.3% (95% CI 84.1% to 91.7%).
text.formatted: On the test situations, direct zero-shot prompting reached an accuracy of 86.3% (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_3">7</ref>), few-shot prompting 87.0%, chain-of-thought 86.3%, the LLM-as-judge 86.7%, and the strict JSON Schema classifier, run with the smaller gpt-oss-20b, 87.7%; the ensemble of three models reached 87.3%, with the three models agreeing on 88% of the situations, and self-consistency, the majority of five answers sampled at a temperature of 0.8, was the most accurate prompted classifier, with 88.3% (95% CI 84.1% to 91.7%).

text.text: Asking the model to verbalize a score for every emotion, rather than to name one, gave the lowest accuracy (83.7%), and none of the 2,700 predictions of the table was an invalid or missing label.

The confidence intervals of all prompted classifiers overlap, so that, with 300 test situations, the prompting strategies are better described as equivalent than as ranked, and the elaborate strategies (examples, reasoning, judges, ensembles, repeated sampling) added at most 2.0 points to the plain instruction while multiplying its cost.

On the same test situations, the cross-validated head on MPNet embeddings classified 84.3% correctly and the head on Voyage AI embeddings 87.7%, so that a generative model given only the names of the four emotions was as accurate as a supervised head trained on 480 labeled situations in each fold.

Sending the situations sorted by emotion left the accuracy practically unchanged (86.0%), so gpt-oss-120b did not exploit the order of the labels in these batches, but the sorted and shuffled runs disagreed on 31 of the 300 situations (10.3%), a variation that also includes the run-to-run variability of the model, since the TEXT CLASSIFICATION WITH LLMCLASSIFICR 52 shuffled run was not repeated.
Whatever the exact numbers, three engineering lessons hold for any study.

First, the order of the texts within a batch is part of the prompt and should be randomized and reported, because the sensitivity to order differs between models and tasks (Lu et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2021) and randomizing it costs nothing.
text.formatted: First, the order of the texts within a batch is part of the prompt and should be randomized and reported, because the sensitivity to order differs between models and tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">(Lu et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b121">Zhao et al., 2021)</ref> and randomizing it costs nothing.

text.text: Second, structured outputs with an enumeration of the allowed classes remove invalid labels by construction, which simplifies the analysis but does not make the labels correct.

Third, every prompt, model identifier, date, and setting (sampling temperature, reasoning effort, batch size) is part of the measurement instrument and must be reported verbatim, since the same prompt may produce different results after a model update (Abdurahman et al., 2024; Ziems et al., 2024).

text.text: Topic discovery addresses the situation in which the categories are not known in advance, or in which a researcher wants to check whether the categories proposed by a theory emerge from the texts.
The package supports two routes, which can be combined.

In the human-guided route, EGA finds communities of texts in an embedding space, the analyst inspects the most typical words and the most central texts of each community, names the communities, writes one description per name, and the descriptions become a zero-shot classifier for the whole corpus.
In the automated route, an LLM reads a set of retrieved documents and proposes the topics and their descriptions (RAG), and the same or another LLM classifies every text into them.

E_mpnet <-readRDS(emb_file("ed_mpnet")) topic_ega <keep("topic_ega_ed", ega_classify(E_mpnet, optimize_steps = TRUE, plot = FALSE)) communities <-topic_ega$communities table(communities, useNA = "ifany") # 2.

text.text: The communities correspond to recurrent kinds of situations (Table 8), such as someone throwing away the writer's lunch, the death of a pet, a relative who needs care, a new job, or a vacation the writer cannot wait for, and most of them are dominated by one emotion, although some mix two, such as one of the two largest communities, about pets, which contains both caring and excitement.
The human-guided step condenses the communities into a small number of themes.
For this illustration, six descriptions were written after reading the typical words and the central situations of the communities: # 3.
Human-guided step: the analyst reads the terms and the central # situations, names the communities and writes one description per # name.
The descriptions define a zero-shot classifier for ALL texts.

text.text: Figure 8 shows where the mapping fails: the theme Good news attracted many situations whose writers chose anger or sadness (23 and 27), which suggests that its description was too general, and Loss also captured 24 caring situations, mostly about the illness, death, or distress of a person or an animal the writer cared for.
