text.text: The descriptions and the mapping were written by an analyst who had access to the labels of the corpus, so the result should be read as an illustration of the workflow rather than as an unbiased estimate of its accuracy; in a real study, the descriptions should be written by researchers blind to the labels, and the mapping between themes and constructs should be decided in advance.

The automated route uses Voyage AI embeddings for retrieval and gpt-oss-120b for the generation of topics and for the classification: Finances collected mostly angry situations (72 of 133), and only Grief corresponded to an emotion (69 of its 95 situations were sad).

Whether an automated pipeline recovers the categories of interest depends on the retrieved documents, which may over-represent some themes (the retrieved situations can be inspected with retrieve_similar()), and on the generality of the request: asking for "topics" yields topics, and asking for "emotions felt by the writers" yields emotions.

The two routes are complementary: the LLM is a fast generator of candidate categories, and the human-guided route keeps the researcher in control of the definitions, which, as the next sections show, are the actual measurement instrument of description-based classifiers.

The Jev functions are written in pure R and send one request per text, in parallel (10 at a time by default), with automatic retries; failed requests are returned as missing values, and every batch reports its duration, failures, tokens, and cost.

A question is built with jev_choice(), jev_noul(), or jev_score(), several questions can be asked about the same text in a single request with jev_ask() and jev_ask_many(), and the wrappers jev_classify(), jev_multilabel(), and jev_rate() return data frames in the common output format.
The criteria are the measurement instrument: the same descriptions used by the Jev-like classifier of Section define the four emotions, which makes the two approaches directly comparable.
The Jev results are reported for all 600 situations, as for the Jev-like classifier, and for the 300 test situations, as for the prompted LLMs.
A Jev request contains a text, called the state, and one or more named questions about it.

The first step builds four questions about one situation from the calibration half, chosen because it involves two emotions: its writer chose caring, but the situation also involves the sadness of a friend.

The Choice question asks which of the four emotions the writer felt and uses the four emotion criteria as its options; the first Noul question asks whether a statement about sadness is true, with no further criteria; the second Noul question adds explicit criteria for when its statement is true and when it is false; and the Score question rates the intensity of the emotion on a rubric with four ordered levels.

Each answer has a structure that depends on its type: a Choice answer contains the selected option, a probability for every option (summing to 1), and a separate confidence value; a Noul answer contains the probability that the statement is true, so that the answers to several Noul questions about the same text need not sum to 1; and a Score answer contains the probability of every level and their probability-weighted average, the score.
For the example situation, Table 10 shows how the three types of questions complement each other.

text.text: The Choice question must assign the situation to one emotion, and it chose caring with a probability of 1.00; the Noul question about caring, with its explicit criteria, agreed (0.98), while the Noul question about sadness, which could have recognized the second emotion of the situation, gave only 0.33, which is a defensible reading of its statement, since the situation describes the sadness of the friend and not that of the writer; and the Score question, at level 2 ("Clear") with a score of 1.88, adds a dimension, intensity, that the categories ignore.

The example also shows that the wording of a Noul statement decides what is being measured: a statement about whether the situation involves sadness, rather than whether the writer felt it, would ask a different question.

The synthetic corpora were easier for Jev as for every other classifier: it classified all 120 extraversion texts correctly (100.0%) and 90.9% of the bios, against 87.0% of the real situations.

The Noul questions, one per emotion and all asked in the same request, separate each emotion from the others with an AUC of 0.98 (anger), 0.94 (caring), 0.98 (excitement), 0.94 (sadness), and 22.8% of the situations have more than one emotion with a probability above 0.5 (Figure 9, left).

text.text: The Score question rates the intensity of the emotion on four behaviorally anchored levels, with mean scores of 1.70 for anger, 1.32 for caring, 1.65 for excitement, 1.76 for sadness (right).
Classifying the 600 situations with the Choice question used 266,130 input tokens, cost US$0.011177, and took 59 seconds.

Three features make Jev attractive for research: its outputs are probabilities by design, so they can be calibrated and certified with the tools of Section ; it does not generate text, so it cannot return an invalid label; and it is fast and cheap enough to serve as a first-pass coder or as a judge of synthetic data (Raschka, 2026).

text.text: It also shares the limitations of every proprietary model: its training data are unknown (so the possibility that public corpora such as EmpatheticDialogues were seen during training cannot be excluded), the texts are sent to an external server, and the model version must be pinned and reported.
A Jev-like classifier needs only an embedding function and one description per class.

The replication script applies classify_by_description() to all corpora with the two sentence encoders, using the descriptions of label_descriptions for the synthetic corpora and the four emotion criteria for the real situations, and, as a test of how much the wording of the descriptions matters, it also classifies the real situations with the descriptions written for the synthetic emotion corpus (renamed to the corresponding real labels). jevlike[, c("encoder", "data", "method", "accuracy")]
Without a single labeled text, the bi-encoder classified the synthetic corpora with accuracies between 76% and 100% (Table 12), MPNet being more accurate than MiniLM in every corpus but one.
text.formatted: Without a single labeled text, the bi-encoder classified the synthetic corpora with accuracies between 76% and 100% (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">12</ref>), MPNet being more accurate than MiniLM in every corpus but one.

text.text: On the real situations, the MPNet classifier with the four emotion criteria reached 81.8%, only 1.50 points below the cross-validated head on the same embeddings, which was trained on 480 labeled situations in each fold, and far above the bag-of-words baseline (64.8%); MiniLM reached 70.8%.

With the embeddings of the commercial services, the same classifier, still without a single labeled situation, reached 83.7% with Voyage AI and 80.3% with Jina AI; the Voyage AI version was as accurate as the supervised head on MPNet embeddings, and on the 300 test situations (86.0%) it was within the range of the prompted LLMs and of Jev, although it needs only one embedding per text and per description, which can be stored and reused for any new set of descriptions.

The wording of the descriptions mattered: the descriptions written for the synthetic emotion corpus, which name the same four emotions in different words, lowered the accuracy on the real situations to 75.3% with MPNet and to 67.0% with MiniLM.
In a description-based classifier the descriptions are the measurement instrument, and, like the items of a questionnaire, they should be piloted, revised, and reported verbatim.

The zero-shot classifier assigns each situation to the description with the largest similarity; the narrow range of the similarities is the reason why their softmax needs a small temperature (Section ).
Figure 10 shows why the classifier works and why its probabilities need care.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure">10</ref> shows why the classifier works and why its probabilities need care.

text.text: For each description, the situations whose writers chose the corresponding emotion have the largest similarities, but the distributions overlap, and all similarities lie in a narrow range (from -0.16 to 0.59), so that the median difference between the largest and the second-largest similarity of a situation is only 0.071.
Could the shared head of a Jev-like classifier learn, from labeled tasks, a weighting of the embedding dimensions that transfers to new tasks?

The script trains the head on two families of synthetic tasks and tests it on the third, and then trains it on all synthetic tasks and tests it on the real situations: Each segment joins the two heads for the same test data and encoder.

The trained head changed little (Table 13 and Figure 11): for the real situations, the accuracy of MPNet was 81.8% with the untrained head and 81.5% with the trained one, although the trained head lowered the ECE from 0.116 to 0.096, and on the held-out synthetic tasks the trained head helped in some cases and hurt in others.

text.text: With only three families of synthetic tasks, the head has little to learn that generalizes, which is consistent with the emphasis that the developers of Jev place on carefully curated synthetic training data (Raschka, 2026).

text.text: The main practical lesson is that the untrained bi-encoder, whose only parameter is the temperature, is already a strong zero-shot classifier, and that its probabilities, as shown next, need calibration.

Cosine similarities between sentence embeddings are small and close to each other, so their softmax at T = 1 is nearly uniform: the Jev-like classifier was right for 82.7% of the test situations while claiming a mean confidence of only 27.4%, an expected calibration error of 0.553 (Table 14).
text.formatted: Cosine similarities between sentence embeddings are small and close to each other, so their softmax at T = 1 is nearly uniform: the Jev-like classifier was right for 82.7% of the test situations while claiming a mean confidence of only 27.4%, an expected calibration error of 0.553 (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">14</ref>).

text.text: The temperature fitted on the calibration half, T = 0.033, sharpened the probabilities and reduced the ECE to 0.056 and the NLL from 1.303 to 0.487, without changing the accuracy, since dividing all scores by the same number does not change which class is largest.
The default of classify_by_description(), T = 0.05, was a reasonable but not an optimal choice for these data (ECE = 0.130), and it should not be trusted for other encoders or texts.

The left panel of Figure 12 shows the NLL as a function of T , with a clear minimum, and the right panel shows the reliability diagrams of the Jev-like classifier with the default and the fitted temperatures, together with that of the logistic head.

text.text: Temperature scaling is not limited to zero-shot scores.

text.text: Jev Choice claimed a mean confidence of 94.0% for an accuracy of 85.7% (ECE = 0.091), and the vote shares of self-consistency a mean confidence of 95.7% for an accuracy of 88.3% (ECE = 0.074; Table 15).
text.formatted: Jev Choice claimed a mean confidence of 94.0% for an accuracy of 85.7% (ECE = 0.091), and the vote shares of self-consistency a mean confidence of 95.7% for an accuracy of 88.3% (ECE = 0.074; Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">15</ref>).

text.text: The confidence of both was informative about which answers were right: Jev gave its choice a probability of at least 0.995 for 63% of the test situations and was right for 95.8% of them, and the five votes of self-consistency were unanimous for 85% of the situations, 95.7% of which were classified correctly, against 47.8% of the others.

The problem lies in the confident errors: 9 of the 43 errors of Jev gave the emotion chosen by the writer a probability below 0.01, which is why its NLL (1.069) was more than twice that of the Jev-like classifier with a fitted temperature (0.487).

The fitted temperatures, T = 1.153 for Jev and T = 1.136 for self-consistency (values above 1 soften the probabilities), reduced the ECE to 0.044 and 0.035 and the NLL to 0.389 and 0.344, the lowest NLL of any classifier in the paper, so that the probabilities of the API-based classifiers, once calibrated on 300 situations from the same population, were the most informative of all.

Calibration answers the question "can the probabilities be taken at face value?", but a researcher who uses classifications as data needs more: which classifications can be accepted automatically and which should be checked by a human, what can be guaranteed about the error rate of the accepted classifications, and whether the uncertainty of the model has anything to do with the uncertainty of human coders.

This section addresses the first two questions with the situations, whose calibration half is used to fit every quantity and whose test half is used to evaluate it; the third is addressed with the rater-labeled comments in Section.

When a classifier is allowed to abstain, the texts it is least confident about can be sent to human coders, and the accuracy among the accepted texts rises as the share of accepted texts (the coverage) decreases (Figure 13).

Selective classification depends only on how the texts are ranked by confidence, so it can be useful even when the probabilities are miscalibrated; calibration matters when a confidence threshold, rather than a coverage, is fixed in advance.

Split conformal prediction certifies coverage: with α = 0.10, the prediction sets built from the calibration situations should contain the true emotion of at least 90% of the test situations, whatever the classifier, provided that calibration and test situations are exchangeable.
Since the two halves were sampled from the same pool, they are exchangeable here, and the empirical coverage on the test half can be compared with the nominal level.

situations with sets of 1.27 emotions on average (74% of them containing a single emotion), and the MPNet head covered 90.0% with sets of 1.17 emotions (82% singletons), while the bag-of-words head needed sets of 2.40 emotions to reach the same coverage: a more accurate classifier needs smaller sets.

The sets were also larger for the situations whose most probable emotion was wrong (1.63 against 1.19 emotions for the Jev-like classifier), so that the size of a set flags the texts that deserve a second look.
The API-based classifiers of Table 15 show both sides of this relation.

text.text: The probabilities of Jev Choice produced the smallest sets among the classifiers whose sets varied in size, 1.08 emotions on average with 92% singletons, at a coverage of 90.0%, while the vote shares of self-consistency, which can take only a few distinct values with five runs, produced a single emotion for every situation, so that the coverage (88.3%, below the nominal 90% in this split) equaled the accuracy and the sets carried no information about ambiguity; more runs, or verbalized scores, would be needed for vote shares to support set-valued classification.

Two details of this single split weaken the guarantee: the probabilities of the heads were obtained by cross-validation over all 600 situations, so that the model that scored a test situation had been trained on calibration situations, and the temperature of the Jev-like classifier was fitted on the same calibration half that sets the conformal threshold; strictly, the scores must be fixed before the calibration texts are seen, which can be achieved by splitting the calibration half in two.

The guarantee also holds only on average over calibration sets, and a single split can fall above or below the nominal level by chance, so the script repeats the analysis with random splits; for the head, which must not see the calibration texts, each split uses separate training (300), calibration (150), and test (150) situations:
The guarantee holds on average over calibration sets.

text.text: This is what certification means in the present context: whatever the classifier, and without any assumption about its calibration, the procedure guarantees the coverage on average, and the cost of a weak classifier is paid in the size of the sets rather than in the validity of the guarantee.
The guarantee rests on exchangeability; thresholds calibrated on synthetic texts, on another platform, or before a model update, offer none.

Every accuracy reported so far measures agreement with a label, and the labels of the situations are as good as labels get: they are the emotions the writers chose for their own situations.

Many corpora used in psychology and the social sciences are instead labeled by raters who read each text after the fact, and the reliability of those labels sets an upper bound on the accuracy that any classifier can demonstrate, since a classifier that agrees with the truth more often than the raters do cannot be recognized as doing so.

text.text: The present paper introduced llmClassificR and used it to dissect eight questions that arise whenever LLMs are used to classify texts in psychological research.

The analyses combined synthetic corpora generated by LLMs, descriptions of emotional situations labeled by their writers, and Reddit comments labeled by several raters, and they point to a small number of conclusions that are likely to generalize beyond the data used here.

Figure 17 condenses the main pattern, by applying the same four classifiers, with the same embeddings and the same emotion descriptions, to the three kinds of data, and Figure 18 sets the main classifiers of the paper side by side on the same 300 test situations.

The first conclusion is that synthetic corpora are excellent for teaching and for prototyping methods, but they are a poor guide to the accuracy of a method on real text.

Every method of Figure 17 was less accurate on the real situations than on the synthetic texts, and all but the bag-of-words head, whose accuracy was essentially unchanged, were less accurate still on the rater-labeled comments; the prime-weight encodings that recovered the synthetic traits and facets with accuracies above 90% (Table 4) recovered the emotions of the situations only partially, and EGA.fit() on MPNet embeddings, the one unsupervised method applied to all three kinds of data, fell from 66.7% on the synthetic texts to 34.7% on the situations and 23.5% on the comments.
text.formatted: Every method of Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_14">17</ref> was less accurate on the real situations than on the synthetic texts, and all but the bag-of-words head, whose accuracy was essentially unchanged, were less accurate still on the rater-labeled comments; the prime-weight encodings that recovered the synthetic traits and facets with accuracies above 90% (Table <ref type="table">4</ref>) recovered the emotions of the situations only partially, and EGA.fit() on MPNet embeddings, the one unsupervised method applied to all three kinds of data, fell from 66.7% on the synthetic texts to 34.7% on the situations and 23.5% on the comments.

text.text: Synthetic texts are generated one category at a time, are prototypical, and repeat the same vocabulary, while real texts serve many purposes at once (Long et al., 2024; Shumailov et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Synthetic texts are generated one category at a time, are prototypical, and repeat the same vocabulary, while real texts serve many purposes at once <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">(Long et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b97">Shumailov et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Synthetic texts can nevertheless serve as training data when the representation generalizes: a head trained agreement between raters, which is rarely reported in text classification studies, should be estimated, and the task defined to match what the raters did, before classifiers are compared (Chen, 2022; Uma et al., 2021).

text.text: The third conclusion concerns the role of network psychometrics and complexity science in LLM-based classification.

When the categories of interest are the dominant structure of the texts, EGA on embeddings recovers them without labels, and the prime-weight encoding of the per-layer networks, which treats a transformer as a multiplex network, was the most accurate label-free method on the synthetic corpora and on the real situations, outperforming, for BERT and the decoder LLM, the more common strategies of averaging or concatenating the layers; its advantage comes from the pairs of texts that are linked consistently across layers (Section ).

When the categories are only one of several organizing principles of the texts, as for the situations, the communities reflect kinds of situations, and the human-guided route of Section shows how they can be turned into a classifier whose categories are defined by the researcher.

The layer-wise comparison of supervised probes and unsupervised EGA (Figure 7) makes the same point from a different angle: information can be linearly readable with labels and still not form communities without them.
text.formatted: The layer-wise comparison of supervised probes and unsupervised EGA (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_14">7</ref>) makes the same point from a different angle: information can be linearly readable with labels and still not form communities without them.

text.text: The embedding services do not change this conclusion: added to the BERT layers, Voyage AI and Jina AI left the label-free solutions practically where they were (Table 5), while the Voyage AI embeddings gave the most accurate supervised head and, with label descriptions, the most accurate description-based classifier.
text.formatted: The embedding services do not change this conclusion: added to the BERT layers, Voyage AI and Jina AI left the label-free solutions practically where they were (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">5</ref>), while the Voyage AI embeddings gave the most accurate supervised head and, with label descriptions, the most accurate description-based classifier.

text.text: The fourth conclusion is that the probabilities attached to LLM-based classifications must be treated as estimates to be checked and, when needed, repaired.

The cosine similarities that drive a Jev-like classifier are on an arbitrary scale, so their softmax at an arbitrary temperature is badly calibrated, and temperature scaling, fitted on a calibration set with a single parameter, repaired the confidence without changing the accuracy, as it did for the under-confident probabilities of a penalized logistic head and for the over-confident probabilities of Jev and of self-consistency, which, once calibrated, had the lowest negative log-likelihood of all classifiers.

Conformal prediction went one step further, turning the probabilities of any classifier into prediction sets with a distribution-free coverage guarantee, which held on average over repeated splits and whose sizes are an interpretable measure of uncertainty, although, on the rater-labeled comments, they were only weakly related to the disagreement between raters, and the multi-label Noul probabilities of Jev, which tracked that disagreement better than the probabilities of the two classifiers forced to choose one emotion, still did so only weakly (Table 18).

text.text: Both procedures depend on the exchangeability between the calibration texts and the texts to be classified, which means that a temperature or a conformal threshold estimated on synthetic texts, or on a different population, offers no guarantee for real texts; the calibration set must come from the population of interest (Angelopoulos & Bates, 2023).

text.text: The fifth conclusion concerns the choice among the families of classifiers (Figure 18).
text.formatted: The fifth conclusion concerns the choice among the families of classifiers (Figure <ref type="figure">18</ref>).

text.text: On the same 300 test situations, the classifiers that saw no labeled situation (apart from the eight examples of the few-shot prompt) and were reached through an API (the prompted LLMs, Jev, and the description-based classifiers on Voyage AI and Jina AI embeddings) were correct for 82.3% to 88.3% of the situations, the supervised heads on the embeddings of local models for 78.7% to 84.3%, and the head on Voyage AI embeddings for 87.7%, with confidence intervals that overlap between the most accurate members of each family; the zero-shot description-based classifier on local MPNet embeddings, which needs neither labels nor an Internet connection, reached 82.7%, within 6 points of the most accurate classifier, and the label-free solutions, at most 53.0%, were far behind.

For a task whose categories can be described in a sentence, the choice among the strong classifiers therefore depends less on accuracy than on cost, on whether the texts may leave the researcher's computer, on whether labeled texts exist, and on the quality of the probabilities, which differed much more than the accuracies (Sections and ).

The comparison also shows the limits of a single corpus of 600 short texts: the differences among the strong classifiers are smaller than the uncertainty of their accuracies, and studies that need to rank them should

The sixth conclusion is practical.

Prompted LLMs, embedding services, and Jev offer remarkable convenience, but they come with engineering obligations that are part of the measurement procedure: randomizing the order of texts in batches, constraining outputs to the allowed classes, reporting prompts, criteria, model versions and dates verbatim, pinning model versions when the provider allows it, estimating costs, and respecting the conditions under which participants' texts can leave the researcher's computer.

text.text: The present study has limitations.

The real data were two corpora of short English texts, the emotions were chosen to mirror one synthetic data set, and caring is only an approximate counterpart of the friendly texts of the synthetic corpus; both subsets retained only texts with a single emotion, which makes the task easier than the multi-label problems of the original corpora; the EmpatheticDialogues writers selected an emotion before describing a situation, which makes their texts more prototypical than spontaneous descriptions of emotional events; and both corpora have been public for years, so they may be part of the training data of the LLMs and embedding models used here (Sainz et al., 2023).
text.formatted: The real data were two corpora of short English texts, the emotions were chosen to mirror one synthetic data set, and caring is only an approximate counterpart of the friendly texts of the synthetic corpus; both subsets retained only texts with a single emotion, which makes the task easier than the multi-label problems of the original corpora; the EmpatheticDialogues writers selected an emotion before describing a situation, which makes their texts more prototypical than spontaneous descriptions of emotional events; and both corpora have been public for years, so they may be part of the training data of the LLMs and embedding models used here <ref type="bibr" target="#b93">(Sainz et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: The results of API-based models depend on model versions that will change, and the results of Jev in particular depend on a proprietary model whose architecture and training data are unknown; one of the models planned for the ensemble was retired before the API analyses were run, so that the cached results distributed with the replication materials are the only exact record of the API-based analyses, and a new run of the script should be expected to differ from them in some predictions.
The human-guided descriptions of Section were written by an analyst with access to the labels and should be replaced by descriptions written blind to them in any substantive application.
The package will continue to evolve.

Planned developments include the submission to CRAN, functions that wrap the conformal and selective classification procedures of Section , local cross-encoder Jev-like classifiers that read the text and the description together, multi-label calibration for Noul-like questions, and tools to compare the uncertainty of models with the disagreement of human coders.
The results in this paper were obtained with R 4.5.3, llmClassificR 0.
2.3, EGAnet 2.5.0, glmnet 5.1, tm 0.7.16, reticulate 1.46.0, httr2 1.3.0, and ggplot2 4.0.3 (Wickham, 2016), on macOS Tahoe 26.5.2.

Local transformer models were run on a CPU with Python 3.11, PyTorch 2.2.2, and transformers 4.48.3, using the Hugging Face models bert-base-uncased, answerdotai/ModernBERT-base, Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B, sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2, and sentence-transformers/all-mpnet-base-v2.

API-based analyses used the Groq models openai/gpt-oss-120b, openai/gpt-oss-20b, and qwen/qwen3.8-27b, Voyage AI voyage-4, Jina AI jina-embeddings-v3, and Jev jev-1.13.0; the date on which they were run is stored in cache/results/api_run_date.rds.

All analyses can be reproduced with the replication script, which reads the cached results when they are present and recomputes them otherwise; without API keys, the script runs every local analysis and skips the API-based ones.

Accuracy on the GoEmotions comments as a function of the share of raters who chose the gold emotion, for three classifiers; numbers above the axis give the number of comments in each group.

The raters of the 600 comments agreed only moderately on whether a comment expressed its gold emotion: on average, 67% of the raters of a comment chose it, only 20% of the comments were labeled unanimously, and a held-out rater chose the emotion preferred by the other raters in 64.1% of the ratings.

The disagreement, however, concerned mostly whether a comment expressed one of the four emotions at all: 33.5% of the individual ratings included none of them (the rater chose another category, such as annoyance or approval, or neutral), and when a rater did choose one of the four emotions, it was the emotion preferred by the other raters in 96.5% of the ratings.
The raters, in other words, rarely confused the four emotions with each other, but often did not see any of them in a comment that other raters labeled with one.

A classifier forced to choose one of the four emotions cannot express this second kind of disagreement, and its accuracy mixes comments whose emotion is clear to every rater with comments that a third or more of the raters did not read as expressing the gold emotion.

The classifiers of Table 17 were far less accurate on the comments than on the situations: the MPNet head reached 72.7%, the bag-of-words head 64.7%, and the zero-shot Jev-like classifier 61.7%, 20 points below its accuracy on the situations with the same descriptions.
text.formatted: The classifiers of Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_21">17</ref> were far less accurate on the comments than on the situations: the MPNet head reached 72.7%, the bag-of-words head 64.7%, and the zero-shot Jev-like classifier 61.7%, 20 points below its accuracy on the situations with the same descriptions.

text.text: Accuracy depended strongly on the agreement between raters (Figure 16): the MPNet head classified 81.7% of the unanimous comments correctly, against 62.1% of the comments on which at most half of the raters chose the gold emotion, many of which most raters did not read as expressing that emotion either.
text.formatted: Accuracy depended strongly on the agreement between raters (Figure <ref type="figure">16</ref>): the MPNet head classified 81.7% of the unanimous comments correctly, against 62.1% of the comments on which at most half of the raters chose the gold emotion, many of which most raters did not read as expressing that emotion either.

text.text: The head trained on the situations transferred poorly to the comments (55.5%), a reminder that labels from different sources are not interchangeable: writers describing their own experiences and raters inferring emotions from Reddit comments use the same four words for different things.

Model uncertainty, finally, tracked human disagreement only weakly: the probability that the head assigned to the gold emotion had a Spearman correlation of 0.12 with the share of raters who chose that emotion (0.10 for the zero-shot classifier), and the conformal sets of the head were barely larger for the divided comments than for the unanimous ones (1.62 against 1.56 emotions), while their coverage in this single split, 86.0%, fell below the nominal 90%, for the reasons discussed in Section .

A classifier Asked one Noul question per emotion, Jev classified 76.3% of the comments correctly when the emotion with the largest probability was taken as its answer (Table 17), more than the cross-validated MPNet head, without a single labeled comment.

text.text: Over all comments, the probability that a comment expresses each emotion had a Spearman correlation of 0.65 (anger), 0.56 (caring), 0.68 (excitement), 0.67 (sadness) with the proportion of raters who chose that emotion (Table 18), but the head trained on majority labels reached broadly similar values (0.60, 0.58, 0.69, 0.56, in the same order), because correlations computed over all comments mostly reflect whether a classifier tells the emotions apart.

text.text: The statistic that isolates disagreement, the correlation between the probability of the gold emotion and the share of raters who chose it, was 0.26 for Jev, against 0.12 for the head and 0.10 for the zero-shot classifier: the Noul probabilities of Jev tracked the disagreement of the raters better than the probabilities of classifiers whose answers must sum to 1, but still weakly.

Studies in which disagreement itself is informative should model it directly, for example with soft labels (Pavlick & Kwiatkowski, 2019; Peterson, Battleday, Griffiths, & Russakovsky, 2019; Uma et al., 2021), and multi-label probabilities of this kind are one way of doing so.

The dashed line marks chance.
on 120 synthetic texts with MPNet embeddings classified 74.0% of the real situations correctly.

Jev showed the same contrast: it classified 100.0% of the synthetic extraversion texts and 90.9% of the synthetic bios correctly, against 87.0% of the real situations, a loss similar to those of the MPNet head and of the zero-shot classifier on the emotion texts.
The second conclusion concerns the labels.
An accuracy is an agreement between a classifier and a set of labels, and it can be no more informative than the labels themselves.

On situations labeled by their writers, the classifiers based on MPNet embeddings agreed with the labels in 82% to 83% of the cases, with or without training data; on comments labeled by raters, the same classifiers were 10 to 20 points less accurate, and the rater-level annotations show why: the raters disagreed mostly about whether a comment expressed one of the four emotions at all, a question that a classifier forced to choose among the four cannot answer.

text.text: Figure 2Four of the 13 networks combined by the prime-weight encoding of the Big Five bios: the TMFG networks of the input embeddings (layer 0) and of BERT layers 4, 8, and 12, with bios colored by their true trait.
Each panel has its own layout; the NMI between the walktrap communities of each layer and the traits is shown in the panel title.
Figure 2 shows four of the 13 networks.

Each has 324 edges (3n -6 for n = 110 bios), but the edges connect different pairs of bios in different layers, and the communities of each layer agree with the traits to a different degree: the NMI between the walktrap communities of a layer and the traits is 0.41 in the input embeddings and 0.74 in the last layer, and it varies without a steady trend in between (from 0.46 to 0.70).
The encoding exploits the consistency of the links across layers.

Of all pairs of bios with the same trait, 49% are linked in at least one layer, against 8% of the pairs with different traits, and, among the linked pairs, same-trait pairs are linked in 5.8 layers on average against 2.2 for different-trait pairs (Figure 3, top left); while only 19% of all pairs share a trait, 91% of the pairs linked in at least 7 of the 13 layers do.

Because each linked layer adds a prime to the encoded value of a pair, these consistently linked pairs carry the largest values of X, and the floor-free network R, ordered by the true traits, shows five blocks along its diagonal (top right).
Figure 3 Inside the prime-weight encoding of the Big Five bios (13 BERT layers).
Top left: number of layers in which a pair of bios is linked, for pairs with the same and with different traits (pairs never linked are omitted).
Top right: floor-free network R, with bios ordered by their true trait (darker cells: pairs linked strongly and in many layers).

Bottom: number of walktrap communities (left) and NMI with the traits (right) for 2 to 25 steps, for the original and the floor-free encodings; the larger points mark the step chosen without labels (the first step that gives the most frequent number of communities).

The options of the Choice question are named, and the names are the labels that the answer will use; a Noul question needs only a statement, although explicit criteria for true and false make its meaning precise, in the same way as the anchors of a rating scale; and the levels of a Score question are listed in order and numbered from 0, with their descriptions acting as behavioral anchors.

text.text: Figure 11Untrained (cosine scores with w = 20) and trained shared heads on tasks the trained head never saw, for MiniLM and MPNet: accuracy (left) and expected calibration error (right).
Two different temperatures appear in LLM-based classification.

The sampling temperature of a generative model controls how random the generated tokens are, and in classification it matters mainly when several answers are sampled (self-consistency), since a higher sampling temperature produces more diverse votes and therefore less extreme vote proportions.
The temperature of temperature scaling is applied after the model, to its scores, and is fitted to make the probabilities honest.

The script fits it on the calibration half of the situations, for the cosine scores of the Jev-like classifier and for the log-probabilities of the logistic head on MPNet embeddings, and evaluates it on the test half. y <-ed$label calib <-ed$split == "calibration" test <-ed$split == "test" emotions <names(emotion_criteria) S <-cosine_scores(text_emb("ed", "mpnet"), label_emb("criteria", "mpnet")) P_head <as.matrix(heads[["MPNet (sentence encoder)"]][, emotions]) T_cos <-fit_temperature(S[calib, ], y[calib]) T_head <-fit_temperature(log(pmax(P_head[calib, ], 1e-8)), y[calib]) c(jevlike = T_cos, head = T_head) temp_table <rbind( calibration_metrics(softmax(S[test, ], 1), y[test], "Jev-like, T = 1"), calibration_metrics(softmax(S[test, ], 0.05), y[test], "Jev-like, T = 0.05 (default)"), calibration_metrics(softmax(S[test, ], T_cos), y[test], "Jev-like, T fitted"), calibration_metrics(P_head[test, ], y[test], "Logistic head, T = 1"), calibration_metrics(softmax(log(pmax(P_head[test, ], 1e-8)), T_head), y[test], "Logistic head, T fitted")) temp_table # Calibration-split negative log-likelihood as a function of T nll_curve <data.frame(T = exp(seq(log(0.005), log(1), length.out = 60))) nll_curve$NLL <sapply(nll_curve$T, function(t) calibration_metrics(softmax(S[calib, ], t), y[calib], digits = 6)$NLL)
